newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bonds sell on Aussie weakness, all eyes on CPI.
newsitem.headline: NZ bonds sell on Aussie weakness, all eyes on CPI.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.60 PCT (PREV 7.65) US 5-YR 6.30 (PREV 6.30) NZD/USD 0.7037/44 (PREV 0.7025/32) US 10-YR 6.52 (PREV 6.52)
* NZ bonds weaken on back of Australian selling
* Day otherwise uneventful
* All eyes on Friday's inflation data for direction
New Zealand bonds sold off at Thursday's close as Australian yields were pushed higher by December quarter employment data that clouded the Australian interest rate outlook.

Headline figures for the December month matched market expectations of a 4,500 rise in employment, and unemployment at 8.6 percent. But employment grew 54,500 in the December quarter, which some analysts said suggested job growth wasn't as weak as people had thought.
New Zealand bonds outperformed Australia, with the three years selling off three points and the 10-year bond off four to 7.29 percent.
Other than the small flurry of activity caused by the Australian data, the session was uneventful, bond dealers said.
Money market traders reported a similar phenomenon.

"It's been pretty quiet really, for the whole day. Just towards the close one guy came out and paid a few in the back end of the bill curve, so that dropped the curve about two points on the day, but, all in all, very quiet," one said.

He said all action was on hold ahead of key inflation data due on Friday at 10.45 a.m. (2145 GMT). With the currency's Trade-Weighted Index up at 68.12, a number even marginally below market expectations would be sufficient to trigger a rally lower in rates.

The Reserve Bank is forecasting December quarter underlying inflation at 0.5 percent for an annual rise of 2.3 percent. A Reuters poll of economists showed the market is more optimistic -- on average they picked a 0.4 percent quarterly rise for an annual rise of 2.15 percent.
The bill dealer said a quarterly rise of 0.4 or 0.5 percent might see a small knee-jerk rally but he doubted it would be sustainable unless the Kiwi dollar was to kick on.
